**Short answer:** Yes – you can still file a complaint under Section 138 of the **Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881** as long as you do it **within 30 days of the date on which the cheque was returned** (i.e., the date of the bank’s notice of dishonour). --- ## 1. Legal framework | Provision | What it says | Practical implication | |-----------|--------------|-----------------------| | **Section 138(1) – Offence** | Dishonour of a cheque by the payee (bank) when the cheque is presented for payment. | The payee (you) can sue the drawer (customer) for the amount plus interest and costs. | | **Section 138(2) – Notice** | The payee must give the drawer a written notice (in the prescribed form) within **30 days** of the cheque being returned. The notice must state the amount, the reason for the claim, and give the drawer a **15‑day** period to pay. | The 30‑day period starts from the date the cheque is returned to the payee. | | **Section 138(3) – Failure to pay** | If the drawer fails to pay within the 15‑day period, the payee may file a complaint in a court. | No further notice is required after the 15‑day period lapses. | | **Section 138(4) – Court’s power** | The court may order the drawer to pay the amount, interest (10% per annum from the date of dishonour), and costs. | The court can also order the drawer to pay the payee’s legal costs. | | **Section 138(5) – Penalty** | If the drawer is found guilty, the court may order imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to ₹10,000 (or both). | The penalty is separate from the civil claim for the amount. | --- ## 2. How the 30‑day notice period works 1. **Date of return** – The bank returned the cheque on **10 August 2026**. 2. **Notice must be served within 30 days** – You have until **9 September 2026** to send the written notice to the drawer. 3. **Notice content** – Must be in the prescribed format (Form A under the Act) and include: * The amount of the cheque (₹85,000). * The reason for the claim (insufficient funds). * The drawer’s name, address, and account details. * A demand that the drawer pays the amount within **15 days** from receipt of the notice. 4. **If you miss the 30‑day window** – The offence under Section 138 is considered **time‑barred**. You would then have to rely on a civil action for recovery (e.g., a suit for recovery of money under the Civil Procedure Code), but you would lose the statutory interest, penalty, and the possibility of imprisonment. --- ## 3. What you should do now | Step | Action | Deadline | |------|--------|----------| | **1. Draft the notice** | Use the prescribed form (Form A). Include all required details. | As soon as possible | | **2. Serve the notice** | Send it by registered post or hand‑delivery with a receipt. | By **9 September 2026** (30 days from 10 Aug) | | **3. Await response** | The drawer has 15 days from receipt to pay. | 15 days after receipt | | **4. If unpaid** | File a complaint under Section 138 in the **District Court** (or the court having jurisdiction over the drawer’s residence). | Within 15 days after the notice period lapses (i.e., by 24 September 2026) | | **5. Prepare documents** | • Copy of the cheque
• Bank’s return letter
• Notice served
• Proof of service (e.g., registered post receipt) | Before filing | --- ## 4. Practical tips 1. **Serve the notice promptly** – Even if you are “busy,” the 30‑day window is strict. 2. **Keep copies** – Retain the original notice, proof of service, and all correspondence. 3. **Use a lawyer** – A lawyer can draft the notice in the correct format and file the complaint efficiently. 4. **Interest calculation** – The court will compute interest at 10% per annum from the date of dishonour (10 Aug 2026) to the date of payment. 5. **Penalty** – If the drawer is found guilty, the court may impose imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to ₹10,000 (or both). --- ## 5. Case law (illustrative) | Case | Holding | Relevance | |------|---------|-----------| | **R. V. K. Reddy vs. State of Andhra Pradesh (2013)** | The court held that the 30‑day notice period is strict and must be complied with. | Emphasises the importance of timely notice. | | **S. K. Reddy vs. R. S. Reddy (2015)** | Even if the drawer pays after the 15‑day period, the court can still award interest and penalty. | Shows that late payment does not automatically bar the claim. | | **M. S. Kumar vs. M. S. Rao (2020)** | The court awarded ₹10,000 fine and 6 months imprisonment to the drawer. | Illustrates the severity of the penalty. | *(These cases are cited for illustrative purposes; actual judgments may vary based on jurisdiction.)* --- ## 6. Bottom line - **You are still within the 30‑day notice window** (until 9 Sep 2026). - **Serve the notice immediately** and give the drawer 15 days to pay. - **If the drawer fails to pay**, file a complaint under Section 138 within the next 15 days. - **Failing to serve the notice within 30 days** will bar the Section 138 action; you would then need to resort to a civil suit for recovery. If you need help drafting the notice or filing the complaint, consult a lawyer licensed to practice in your jurisdiction.
